# Optimal Site Generator Distribution

**Data Sources: Vodacom data, localized for the Cape Town**

#### Problem Statement 

Load shedding and insecure power supply put a strain on network servicing sites, affecting coverage and availability of those sites with material impact on site revenue generation from user traffic flows. Running generators at sites impacted by power disruptions offers the immediate solution to ensuring sites continue to run during interrupted power supply; however, there is a limited supply of generators that can be deployed to sites, as well as the cost associated with the deployment and running of the generators. Vodacom would like to develop a strategy for the optimal distribution of generators to important sites with the minimum cost attached whilst ensuring coverage needs and availability are maintained.

Key Definitions:

-   Atoll Site ID: Identifier for a physical structure that houses antennas, transmitters, receivers, and networking hardware needed to transmit and receive voice, data, and internet signals. These have a set coverage shape that defines the span of the site's coverage over a physical space (word this better and add refrence)

-   Site Availability: The percentage of time that a specific telecom site, including its radio equipment, power supplies, backhaul, and virtual or physical connection links, is fully operational and capable of processing traffic. (<https://medium.com/>@saeedfelegari/site-availability-in-telecom-metrics-architecture-and-the-real-requirements-behind-the-numbers-37cf574ba711.

    -   This metric is measured as the percentage number of seconds a site is operational over the total number of seconds in a month, with 100%= full availability.

# Section 1: Deterministic MLP Formulation

The generator deployment problem lends itself to the set covering formulation. In this case, we would like to deploy generators the minimum number of sites (and the associated cost) subject to the constraint is \>=95% and at least 90% of total subscribers at full peak/availability can access the network during times of load shedding.

To necessitate this, a few key assumptions have to made:

-   Each site can get only one generator. All cells for each technology (2G,3G,4G,5G) are fully powered by said generator on the site.

-   The cost associated with running a generator is entirely captured by the fuel cost, thus transportation costs are disregarded for now as the generator is deployed once at a site, if that site is chosen. \* get the average cost of fueling and running a mobile generator for n hours

-   We model for Stage 1 load shedding schedule with at most 1 power outage per day for 2hrs .Load shedding affects all sites at the same time. Load shedding happens at peak hours/demand across sites.

-   Average site coverage perimeter=4.24KM, and these site coverage overlap if they are withing this distance of each other. This Site $j$ can serve the subscribers of site $i$ if $d_{ij} \le R$, were R=4.24KM. A site always covers itself.

-   Subscriber location. All subscribers of site $i$ are treated as located at site $i$, so they are either entirely within reach of a powered site or not. This assumes concentrated subscriber densities.

-   Subscribers can connect coverage/network of neighboring sites fluidly (if they are within the average site perimeter). Thus is if one site goes one, and another site within the overlap radius has a generator, then the a subscriber within that radius can access the generator-ran site's network/coverage with no signal degradation at site edges.

-   Unlimited absorption. A powered site can absorb all subscribers of every site within its radius, with no capacity limit.

-   Peak demand. $w_i$ is the subscriber count at site $i$ at full peak. Coverage target. At least 90% of total peak subscribers must be served during the outage.

What I need: Coverage matrix to get the distances between sites.

## Partial Set Covering Formulation

### Sets and parameters

$$
\begin{aligned}
I &: \text{set of sites, indexed by } i, j \\
d_{ij} &: \text{distance between sites } i \text{ and } j \text{ (km)} \\
R &: \text{coverage perimeter (km)} \\
a_{ij} &=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } d_{ij} \le R \quad (\text{so } a_{ii} = 1) \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
w_i &: \text{peak unique subscribers at site } i \\
\beta &= 0.90 : \text{minimum fraction of total subscribers that must be served}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Decision variables

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_j &\in \{0,1\} && \text{1 if a generator is deployed at site } j \\
y_i &\in \{0,1\} && \text{1 if the subscribers of site } i \text{ are served during the outage}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Model

Minimize the number of generators deployed:

$$
\min \sum_{j \in I} x_j
$$ {#eq-obj}

subject to

$$
y_i \le \sum_{j \in I} a_{ij}\, x_j \qquad \forall i \in I
$$ {#eq-cover}

$$
\sum_{i \in I} w_i\, y_i \ge \beta \sum_{i \in I} w_i
$$ {#eq-target}

$$
x_j \in \{0,1\}, \quad y_i \in \{0,1\} \qquad \forall i, j \in I
$$ {#eq-domain}

### Interpretation

@eq-cover states that the subscribers of site $i$ can be served only if some site within radius $R$ of $i$ (including $i$ itself) has a generator - which is the **set covering constraint.** @eq-target requires the served subscribers to total at least a fraction $\beta$ of all subscribers. @eq-obj minimizes the number of generators deployed.

```{r, neigh_matrix}

#Neighbourhood matrix of sites (symmetric) that only populates 1 if two sites are within R/perimetr distance of each other- thus they overlap and 0 otherwise

sites=site_gdf %>%  select (atoll_site_id)

dist_matrix =st_distance(sites) 
dist_matrix=as.matrix(units::set_units(dist_matrix, "km"))
# apply neighbourhood condition

R=units::set_units(4.24,'km')

neigh_mat=ifelse(dist_matrix<= R,1,0)

# matrix(neigh_mat,nrow=)
dim(neigh_mat)

 # Check if matrix is symmetrix
isSymmetric(neigh_mat)

```

# Section 2: Deterministic MOLP Formulation- Revenue and Site Rankings

## Site importance and multi-objective extension

### Additional parameters

Let $R_i$ and $T_i$ denote the revenue and traffic of network site $i \in I$. Normalise each KPI to $[0,1]$:

$$
\tilde{R}_i = \frac{R_i - \min_k R_k}{\max_k R_k - \min_k R_k},
\qquad
\tilde{T}_i = \frac{T_i - \min_k T_k}{\max_k T_k - \min_k T_k}.
$$

The composite importance score of site $i$ is

$$
s_i = \theta\, \tilde{R}_i + (1-\theta)\, \tilde{T}_i,
\qquad \theta \in [0,1],
$$

where $\theta$ sets the relative emphasis on revenue versus traffic. Alternatively, if only the ordinal rank $\rho_i \in \{1,\dots,N\}$ is used (1 = highest revenue), a rank-based weight is

$$
s_i = \frac{N - \rho_i + 1}{N}
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
s_i = \frac{1}{\rho_i}.
$$

The total importance of the network is $S = \sum_{i \in I} s_i$. Sites with $s_i$ in the top tier are collected in the set $I^{\text{top}} \subseteq I$ (for example, the top 10% by revenue rank).

### Model C: weighted-sum objective

Using the same decision variables $x_j$ (generator placed at site $j$) and $y_i$ (site $i$ is covered) as before, let $C = \sum_{j \in J} c_j$ be the cost of deploying at every candidate site (used for scaling). Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & (1-\lambda)\,\frac{1}{C}\sum_{j \in J} c_j\, x_j
\;-\; \lambda\,\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i \in I} s_i\, y_i \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.} \quad
& y_i \le \sum_{j \in J} a_{ij}\, x_j && \forall\, i \in I, \\
& \sum_{i \in I} w_i\, y_i \;\ge\; \alpha \sum_{i \in I} w_i, \\
& y_i = 1 && \forall\, i \in I^{\text{top}} \quad \text{(optional)}, \\
& x_j \in \{0,1\}, \; y_i \in \{0,1\},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda \in [0,1]$ trades off cost against protected importance. Both terms are scaled to $[0,1]$ so that $\lambda$ has a meaningful interpretation. At $\lambda = 0$ the model reduces to Model A.

### Model D: $\varepsilon$-constraint (cost minimisation with an importance floor)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & \sum_{j \in J} c_j\, x_j \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.} \quad
& y_i \le \sum_{j \in J} a_{ij}\, x_j && \forall\, i \in I, \\
& \sum_{i \in I} w_i\, y_i \;\ge\; \alpha \sum_{i \in I} w_i, \\
& \sum_{i \in I} s_i\, y_i \;\ge\; \beta\, S, \\
& x_j \in \{0,1\}, \; y_i \in \{0,1\},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\beta \in [0,1]$ is the minimum fraction of total weighted revenue/traffic that must be protected. This is equivalent to Model C but gives the decision-maker a directly interpretable target. Varying $\beta$ (and $\alpha$) traces the Pareto frontier of cost against protected importance.

### Model E: lexicographic (priority-ordered) objectives

Stage 1 solves Model A to obtain the minimum cost $z_1^*$. Stage 2 fixes cost at (or within a tolerance $\delta$ of) the optimum and maximises protected importance:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & \sum_{i \in I} s_i\, y_i \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.} \quad
& \sum_{j \in J} c_j\, x_j \le (1+\delta)\, z_1^*, \\
& \text{all constraints of Model A.}
\end{aligned}
$$

This guarantees that, among all cost-minimal (or near cost-minimal) deployments, the one protecting the most important sites is chosen.

### Optional: favouring important generator locations

If you also want the *chosen generator sites themselves* to be high-ranked, add a term in the site-selection variables, with $s_j$ the importance score of candidate site $j$:

$$
\max \quad \sum_{i \in I} s_i\, y_i \;+\; \gamma \sum_{j \in J} s_j\, x_j,
\qquad \gamma \ge 0 .
$$

## Option F

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad Z ={}&
\lambda_R \sum_{j \in J} \widetilde{r}_j x_j
+ \lambda_S \sum_{j \in J} s_j x_j
- \lambda_C \sum_{j \in J} \widetilde{g}_j x_j
\\[8pt]
\text{subject to} \quad
& \sum_{k \in K} w_k y_k
\geq \alpha \sum_{k \in K} w_k
\\[6pt]
& y_k \leq \sum_{j \in J} C_{kj} x_j,
&& \forall k \in K
\\[6pt]
& \sum_{j \in J} x_j \leq G
\\[6pt]
& x_j \in \{0,1\},
&& \forall j \in J
\\[4pt]
& y_k \in \{0,1\},
&& \forall k \in K
\end{aligned}
$$

where\

-   $J$: Set of candidate sites where generators could be deployed.
-   $K$: Set of geographic cells used to represent the coverage area.
-   $x_j \in \{0,1\}$: Binary decision variable equal to 1 if a generator is deployed at site $j$, and 0 otherwise.
-   $y_k \in \{0,1\}$: Binary indicator equal to 1 if geographic cell $k$ retains adequate network coverage during load shedding, and 0 otherwise.
-   $C_{kj} \in \{0,1\}$: Coverage indicator equal to 1 if site $j$, when operational, provides adequate coverage to cell $k$, and 0 otherwise.
-   $w_k$: Area weight of geographic cell $k$.
-   $\alpha$: Minimum required proportion of the total geographic area that must retain adequate coverage.
-   $G$: Maximum number of generators available for deployment.
-   $\widetilde{r}_j$: Normalised revenue associated with site $j$.
-   $s_j$: Normalised importance score for site $j$, derived from its business ranking.
-   $\widetilde{g}_j$: Normalised generator deployment cost at site $j$.
-   $\lambda_R, \lambda_S, \lambda_C \geq 0$: Objective weights representing the relative importance of revenue, site ranking, and generator cost, respectively.

# Section 3: Simulated Annealing Formulation\*

Let the candidate solution be represented by a binary vector:

### Simulated Annealing Formulation

Let the candidate solution be represented by a binary vector:

$$
\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n), \qquad x_j \in \{0,1\}, \quad j = 1,\ldots,n
$$

where (x_j = 1) indicates that a generator is deployed at site (j), and (x_j = 0) otherwise.

The initial solution is denoted by\
\
$$
\mathbf{x^{0}} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)
$$

At each iteration (t), a neighbouring solutio is generated by modifying the current solution. For example,

$$
\mathbf{x}^{(t)} = (1,0,0,1,1)
$$

could generate the neighbouring solution

$$
\mathbf{x}' = (0,0,0,1,1)
$$

The objective function is evaluated at the current and neighbouring solutions. For the initial set-covering problem, the objective is to minimise the total number of generators deployed:

$$
\min_{\mathbf{x}} \quad f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} x_j
$$

The simulated annealing algorithm uses the change in objective value,

$$
\Delta f = f(\mathbf{x}') - f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\right)
$$

to determine whether the neighbouring solution should be accepted, with the acceptance decision also depending on the current temperature.

# Discretizing the Problem: Stochastic Load Shedding Scheduling

What is different:\
One of my key assumptions initial LP formulation is that the load shedding schedule is deterministic and that all sites are experiance power outages at the same time. In reality this is not the case.

There is a stochastic element to the prevalence of the power outages and as such not all sites will experiance interrupted power at the same time and require generators. In light of this I want to model the problem as a discrete event and run simulations based on the appropriate statistical distributions of the loadshedding event.

Key Assumptions:

-   The loadshedding stage for a given day is stochastic and as such follows an appropriate statistical distribution, however, the actual load shedding times that come as a result of that announced stage are deterministic and follow a set schedule.

-   Only a percetange of sites are affected by load shedding at the same time. The percentage at any given schedule is itself either stochatistic or determisitic (still to be decided.

### Stochastic Load shedding stage use ditribution of stage frequencies

Stage announcements occur at random epochs. At the $n$-th announcement, at time $T_n$, $$
\sigma(T_n^{+}) = l \quad \text{with probability } p_{\sigma(T_n^{-})\, l},
\qquad
T_{n+1} - T_n \sim F_{S}(\,\cdot \mid \sigma(T_n^{+})),
$$ where $P = [p_{kl}]$ is a stage transition matrix and $F_S(\cdot \mid k)$ is the sojourn-time distribution of stage $k$ (the time until the next announcement), both estimated from historical stage logs. The special case of one announcement per day at a fixed time of day, with $\sigma_d \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \pi$, is obtained by setting $F_S = \delta_{24\text{ h}}$ and $p_{kl} = \pi_l$.

### Deterministic timetable

Given the stage $k$ and the current position in the rotation cycle, the timetable defines, for each block $g$, a set of scheduled off-intervals $$
\mathcal{W}_g^{k}(\delta) = \big\{ [\underline{w}_{g,m}^{k},\, \overline{w}_{g,m}^{k}) \big\}_{m},
$$ within cycle day $\delta$. A stage change at time $T_n$ cancels all pending timetable events and reschedules the intervals of the new stage that begin at or after $T_n$. If $T_n$ falls inside an interval of the new stage in which block $g$ is already scheduled off, block $g$ goes off at $T_n$. An optional switching delay $\epsilon \sim F_\epsilon$ (default $\epsilon = 0$) can be added to each switch-on or switch-off, which gives a controlled way to introduce schedule deviation later.

### Event types and transition rules

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\hline
\textbf{Event} & \textbf{Trigger} & \textbf{State change and scheduled follow-ups} \\
\hline
$E_1$: stage announcement & time $T_n$ & draw new stage; cancel and reschedule $E_2,E_3$ \\
$E_2$: block switch-off & timetable & $u_g \leftarrow 1$; sites on battery; schedule $E_4$ \\
$E_3$: block switch-on & timetable & $u_g \leftarrow 0$; sites on grid; begin battery recharge \\
$E_4$: battery depletion at $i$ & $b_i$ reaches $b_i^{\min}$ & site on generator if available, else down \\
$E_5$: generator fuel exhaustion & $f_j$ reaches 0 & reassign sites; site down if none available \\
$E_6$: end of horizon & $t = H$ & stop and record statistics \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

### Continuous state evolution between events

Between consecutive events the energy states evolve linearly, so no time-stepping is needed. For a site on battery with load $l_i$, $$
b_i(t) = b_i(t_0) - l_i\,(t - t_0), \qquad
t^{\text{depl}}_i = t_0 + \frac{b_i(t_0) - b_i^{\min}}{l_i},
$$ and the depletion event $E_4$ is scheduled at $t^{\text{depl}}_i$. For generator $j$ serving the set $A_j(t)$ of sites, $$
f_j(t) = f_j(t_0) - \Big(\sum_{i \in A_j} l_i\Big)(t - t_0).
$$ After grid restoration a battery recharges at rate $r_i$ up to $B_i$.

### Generator allocation rule

When site $i$ needs backup (battery depleted, or by policy at block switch-off) it is assigned to a generator in $$
J_i(t) = \Big\{ j \in J^x : a_{ij} = 1,\;
f_j(t) > 0,\; \sum_{i' \in A_j(t)} l_{i'} + l_i \le K_j \Big\},
$$ using a priority rule, for example highest importance $s_i$ first and ties broken by nearest generator. If $J_i(t) = \emptyset$ the site is down (unserved) until power or capacity becomes available.

### Event-list algorithm

\begin{enumerate}
\item Initialise $t \leftarrow 0$, $\mathbf{S}(0)$, and the event list $\mathcal{L}$
with the first stage announcement $E_1$ at $T_1$ and the timetable events
for the initial stage.
\item While $\mathcal{L} \neq \emptyset$:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item pop the event $e^{*} = \arg\min_{e \in \mathcal{L}} \tau_e$ and set $t \leftarrow \tau_{e^*}$;
  \item update accumulators over $[t_{\text{prev}}, t]$ using the state held constant
        during the interval (see below);
  \item apply the transition rule of $e^{*}$, reallocate generators, and update $\mathbf{S}$;
  \item schedule new events (depletion, exhaustion, next announcement, timetable
        events) and cancel events invalidated by the state change.
  \end{enumerate}
\item Stop at $t = H$ and return the performance measures.
\end{enumerate}

### Performance measures (per replication $r$)

Let $\mathbb{1}\{\mu_i(t) = \text{down}\}$ indicate that site $i$ is unserved at time $t$. Then \begin{align*}
\text{Downtime of site } i:\quad & D_i^{(r)} = \int_0^H \mathbb{1}\{\mu_i(t) = \text{down}\}\,dt,\\
\text{Importance-weighted unserved exposure:}\quad & L^{(r)} = \sum_{i \in I} s_i\, D_i^{(r)},\\
\text{Revenue lost:}\quad & \Lambda^{(r)} = \sum_{i \in I} R_i\, D_i^{(r)},\\
\text{Generator utilisation:}\quad & \rho_j^{(r)} = \frac{1}{H}\int_0^H \mathbb{1}\{A_j(t) \ne \emptyset\}\,dt,\\
\text{Fuel used:}\quad & \Xi_j^{(r)} = F_j - f_j(H) + \text{refuel quantities}.
\end{align*}

### Replications and output analysis

Run $N$ independent replications $r = 1,\dots,N$ with independent random-number streams. For any measure $Y^{(r)}$, $$
\bar{Y} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{r=1}^{N} Y^{(r)},
\qquad
\bar{Y} \pm t_{N-1,\,1-\gamma/2}\,\frac{S_Y}{\sqrt{N}},
\qquad
S_Y^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{r=1}^{N}\big(Y^{(r)} - \bar{Y}\big)^2 .
$$ The number of replications is chosen so that the relative half-width is at most a target $\varepsilon_{\text{rel}}$: $$
N \;\ge\; \left(\frac{t_{N-1,\,1-\gamma/2}\, S_Y}{\varepsilon_{\text{rel}}\, \bar{Y}}\right)^{2}.
$$ When comparing alternative placements $x$ and $x'$, use common random numbers (the same stage paths in both runs) and a paired confidence interval on $Y^{(r)}(x) - Y^{(r)}(x')$.

### Coupling the simulation with the optimisation

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Scenario generation:} use the simulated outage histories
$o_{i t}^{(r)}$ as the scenario set $\Omega$ in the SAA model.
\item \textbf{Solve} for $x^{*}$.
\item \textbf{Evaluate:} re-run the DES with $x^{*}$ fixed, including battery,
fuel and allocation dynamics, on fresh replications. Report $\bar L$, $\bar\Lambda$ and
tail quantiles, and compare with the optimisation's predicted values.
\end{enumerate}

The gap between optimised and simulated performance measures quantifies the effect of the dynamics omitted from the optimisation model.
